glosses: Anything broad and flexible that hangs loose, or that is attached by one side or end and is easily moved.

glosses: A hinged surface on the trailing edge of the wings of an aeroplane, used to increase lift and drag.
A side fin of a ray.
The motion of anything broad and loose, or a sound or stroke made with it.

examples.text: the flap of a sail
the flap of a wing

Then he commenced to talk, really talk. and inside of two flaps of a herring's fin he had me mesmerized, like Eben Holt's boy at the town hall show. He talked about the ills of humanity, and the glories of health and Nature and service and land knows what all.

glosses: A controversy, scandal, stir, or upset.

examples.text: The comment caused quite a flap in the newspapers.

“[…] We saw him vanish right in front of the rest of us. He was there and then he wasn’t. We were to wait for a year for his return or for some message. We waited. Nothing.” / Calvin, his voice cracking: “Jeepers, sir. You must have been in sort of a flap.”

The current Middlesex grand jury […] is once again on the case, partly as the result of the public flap created by Brill's death and, of course, by the series of articles written by Corsetti in the month after Brill's demise.

glosses: A consonant sound made by a single muscle contraction, such as the sound /ɾ/ in the standard American English pronunciation of body.
A piece of tissue incompletely detached from the body, as an intermediate stage of plastic surgery.
The labia, the vulva.
A blow or slap (especially to the face).

examples.text:
1450, Palladius on Husbondrieː
Ware the horn and heels lest they fling a flap to thee.

a1500 The Prose Merlinː
The squire lift up his hand and gave him such a flap that all they in the chapel might it hear.

glosses: A young prostitute.

examples.text: Fall to your flap, my Masters, kisse and clip. […] Come hither, you foule flappes.

To move (something broad and loose) up and down.

examples.text: The crow slowly flapped its wings.
Startled, the wood pigeon flew off, its wings flapping noisily.
He could be flapping his tongue about you right this minute to anybody who'll bloody listen.

glosses: To move loosely back and forth.

examples.text: The flag flapped in the breeze.

examples.text: Former Turkey goalkeeper Rustu Recber flapped at his first Delap throw but was given a soft free-kick by referee Antony Gautier.

glosses: To pronounce (something) as a flap consonant.

glosses: A thin, narrow strip or bar of wood (lath), metal, or plastic.

examples.text: To keep people out, the Nature Conservancy, which owns the cave, has blocked off the entrance with huge iron slats.

glosses: A control surface that extends forwards and downwards from the leading edge of a wing, leaving a gap between it and the leading edge, in order to modify the airflow around the wing so as to allow flight at a higher angle of attack without stalling, lowering the aircraft's stall speed.
A ski.

examples.text: I never got down that hill without losing at least one of my skis! Clarence didn't lose his slats. The straps went over his boots and held them in place. If he fell, he risked breaking a foot or leg, but the slats stayed on.

glosses: A thin piece of stone; a slate.
A drop (of rain or water), a splash.

examples.text: […] slats of rain broke upon the surface.
A slat of rain drove into his face. It was pitch dark but the sea was calmer and the bucking of the ship had lessened.
[…] a slat of rain. The River-Woman grasped the pouch with her left hand and touched the mouth of it with her right.

[…] a slat of rain and wind gusts which whitened the water where the river made its bend. Then the squall was gone as swiftly as it had come and the sun began to break through the clouds as Mike went slowly along the trail.

glosses: To construct or provide with slats.
To slap or strike; to beat, pummel; to hurl or throw down violently.

examples.text: Men[dozo]. How did you kill him? / Mal[evole]. Slatted his braines out, then ſowſt him in the brinie ſea. / Men. Braind him and drownd him too?

glosses: To throw (something, especially water or liquid) down; to slam or splash (something) down.

examples.text: […] a nudge o' kissing-crust After thy leeky broth: I've warmed thy porridge on tha trivet, Jimmy, zay prayers avore 'e have it, And doant 'e slat tha clath.
[…] slatting water over everything in the dory.
[…] by the sound she knew that he was slatting water from his oilskins. "Thanks. A wet day, sir." The door closed. He must have entered without invitation and shut the door behind him.
Mac stood over me, slatting water off his arms, his face purple.
The hose came in hand over hand, as the sailormen say, and in a few moments the end came switching down on them, slatting water in all directions.

glosses: To fall; to beat (against something).

examples.text: […] sending solid grey water slatting against her wheelhouse windows.
[…] water slatting over the rail. The salt caked on her face and when the sun came up, it was as though her face was being pot-roasted - with salt.

glosses: To split; to crack.

glosses: To set on; to incite.
